narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 50.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

Three factors drove this decision, ranked by importance. First, your family income level in the lower-middle bracket worked in your favor; students from this background are relatively rare in the admitted group, and the model saw this as slightly increasing your likelihood of passing. However, two stronger factors pushed the prediction in the opposite direction. Your LSAT score of 24 is substantially below the average of 37 among accepted students, and this low performance was the most powerful reason the model expected you to struggle with the bar exam. Next, your third-year grades placed you in the second decile of your class, well below the average of roughly sixth decile for those who were admitted. This weaker academic standing in later law school years further increased the predicted risk of failure.

Taken together, the negative influence from your LSAT and upper-year grades outweighed the modest positive signal from your family background, producing a prediction that crossed the rejection line.

You should focus on raising your LSAT score through intensive preparation and consider strengthening your academic performance if you retake any courses. Improving either of these areas would likely shift future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
